claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles maintain a single-phase solid-solution structure from 473 K to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
High-melting-point constituent elements have limited atomic diffusion.
Limited atomic diffusion kinetically hinders elemental segregation.
When atomic migration is insufficient, nanoparticles remain in a kinetically stabilized single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles containing a higher proportion of low-diffusivity, high-melting-point elements will retain a single-phase structure across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles containing a larger proportion of fast-diffusing constituents are more likely to segregate at higher temperatures.
At approximately 473 K, atomic mobility is minimal.
All tested nanoparticles will retain their initial single-phase solid solution at approximately 473 K.
Strongly reactive atmospheres may produce stability behavior different from that predicted under inert or mildly reactive atmospheres.
Changes in nanoparticle size may alter structural and chemical stability.
Surface diffusion effects dominate for the nanoparticle sizes covered by the proposed conditions.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis broadly states that high-entropy alloy nanoparticles maintain their single-phase structure across the operating-temperature range, whereas the predicted outcome says compositions richer in fast-diffusing constituents may segregate at high temperature. The former is insufficiently qualified as a composition-dependent prediction.
